John F. Kennedy. On November 22, 1963, the president was shot and killed in Dallas, Texas during a presidential motorcade, allegedly by Lee Harvey Oswald.

The assassination occurred in Dealey Plaza as Kennedy rode in an open-topped car. His wife, Jackie Kennedy, was beside him. Kennedy was struck multiple times and pronounced dead at Parkland Memorial Hospital at one p.m. local time. Jackie's composed behavior and her attempts to aid her dying husband were captured on film and etched into public memory.

Oswald was a former Marine who fired from the Texas School Book Depository. He was arrested but killed two days later by nightclub owner Jack Ruby while in police custody. The Warren Commission, appointed to investigate, concluded in 1964 that Oswald acted alone, firing three shots from the Book Depository. But the single-bullet theory, which holds that Oswald's second shot passed through both Kennedy and Governor Connally, remains disputed. The House Select Committee on Assassinations in 1979 concluded a conspiracy was likely, reviving doubt about the Warren Commission's findings.

The assassination occurred during the Cold War and heightened U.S.-Soviet tensions. Conspiracy theories swirl around possible Soviet, Cuban, or mob involvement. The assassination was broadcast to the nation, and the Zapruder film, amateur footage of the shooting itself, made it the first major U.S. event whose details could be rewatched and analyzed infinitely. This fueled both investigation and speculation. The Kennedy assassination became the defining example of how a single violent act can fracture a nation's narrative and spawn parallel historical interpretations. It inaugurated the modern conspiracy-theory ecosystem and raised permanent questions about institutional transparency, the Warren Commission's credibility, and the limits of forensic certainty. In American memory, it is inseparable from Cold War anxieties, the 1960s cultural shift, and the mythology of the Kennedy family.
